payload.headline: Microsoft rebounds 1.65% to 492.5, back above support; hold, swing entry triggered

summary.thesis: Microsoft's sales and margins keep improving, but free cash flow has fallen while heavy spending continues, so the stock looks cheap against its own history and expensive on cash flow.
summary.decision: Long-term: hold and add only lower. Swing: enter, because the price closed back above the 491.22 trigger set in the last note.
summary.act_at: Swing entry 491.22, stop 480.69, target 503.99; long-term add at 475.73

payload.happening: Microsoft rose 1.65% to 492.5. That put it back above the top of its 486.0–491.22 support zone, a few days after it broke below that zone. The only news since the last note is a CNBC report of a government official warning of 'bumps in the road' after tech outages, and the report does not name Microsoft. The next earnings report is due 2027-01-27.
payload.business: The latest filing, dated 2026-10-28, shows a business that is still speeding up. Quarterly revenue grew 18.8% from a year earlier, compared with 18.3% two quarters ago. Operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) rose to 47.1% from 46.27%. Analysts raised next-year earnings per share to 24.2, up 2.2% in 30 days. The weak point is cash. Trailing free cash flow (cash left after capital spending) fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and the filings say each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year, down from 51¢ three years ago. In other words, the heavy spending has not paid back yet. That spending is the real business risk. Demand and margins are not at risk on current data. The balance sheet is not at risk either: net cash is 29.0B and the share count shrank 0.27% over the year. The outage news and the tech-sector fear flagged by the macro read affect sentiment, not Microsoft's revenue or margins.

worth.text: The valuation methods disagree sharply. A cash-flow model starts from today's 60.0B of free cash flow, assumes growth fades to 3% by year 10, and discounts at 10.0%. It gives 180.81 to 288.62 per share, with 218.43 in the middle. For the cash-flow model to justify today's price, free cash flow would have to start growing about 40.0% a year. The model caps starting growth at 30%, and even that gives only 343.43. Measured against its own past, the stock is cheap. Its price-to-sales ratio of 10.6 is at the 28th percentile of its own 5-year range, and that history gives 475.73 to 592.92, with 535.43 in the middle. Against peers it is expensive: the peer median price-to-sales is 3.4. Earnings multiples sit in between, at 25.7 times trailing earnings and 20.4 times next year's earnings. The gap between methods comes down to one input: whether the shrunken 60.0B cash base is temporary. I use the own-history range from 475.73 to 535.43, because current earnings and margins support it. The cash-flow figures are the downside reminder if that bet fails.
worth.key_assumption: The spending that cut free cash flow from 78.0B to 60.0B turns back into cash, so next-year earnings (estimate 24.2) are the right basis for value, not today's cash flow.

bull: Revenue growth picked up to 18.8% year over year, from 18.3% two quarters ago, and operating margin rose to 47.1% from 46.27%.
Analysts raised next-year EPS to 24.2, up 2.2% in 30 days. That puts the stock at 20.4 times next year's earnings.
Price-to-sales sits at the 28th percentile of its own 5-year range, and the price is close to the 475.73 low end of its historical fair range.
bear: Free cash flow fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and the filings say returns on investment dropped to 30¢ per dollar from 51¢.
The cash-flow model's base value is 218.43, and today's price requires about 40.0% starting cash-flow growth.
Price-to-sales is 10.6 versus a peer median of 3.4, which leaves little room for a miss. If operating margin fell to 35%, the model value would be 178.34.

levels.what: Today's close is inside the fair range and back above support. Nothing here calls for selling, and it is not cheap enough to add.
Bottom of the own-history fair range, inside the 472.2–480.69 support zone (3 touches). Add here.
Bottom of the lower support zone. A close below it breaks both support zones and the fair range. In that case, make no new adds until the 2027-01-27 report.

longterm.why: The business is improving and estimates are rising, but free cash flow is shrinking and two of three valuation measures lean expensive, so the plan is to hold and add only near 475.73.

swing.why: The close of 492.5 cleared 491.22, the trigger set in the last note. That puts the 486.0–491.22 zone (8 touches) back underneath as support. The target is the bottom of the 503.99–512.76 resistance. The stop sits under the 472.2–480.69 zone's top. That allows more than one 16.98 average daily range of room. Note that the 20-day average (520.09) is still falling.

decision.timing: The swing target sits well inside the 2026-12-18 options window, which prices a 9.3% move. Any swing position should be closed before the 2027-01-27 report, which the 2027-02-19 options price at a 15.4% move. Long-term money beyond the 475.73 add waits for that report's free cash flow figure.

change_mind: A close below 472.2 would cancel the swing and pause long-term adds until the 2027-01-27 report.

If the 2027-01-27 report shows trailing free cash flow still at or below 60.0B, or operating margin back below 46.27%, the fair range would shift toward the 218.43 cash-flow value and the action would become wait.
A close above 512.76 (top of the first resistance zone) would turn the swing target into the 514.63–518.87 zone, and the long-term view would move toward the 535.43 mid value.
payload.what_changed: Changed: the swing moved from wait to enter because the close of 492.5 recovered the 491.22 trigger, while the long-term hold is unchanged, still supported by the 47.1% operating margin and the next-year EPS estimate rising to 24.2.
payload.label: Research, not advice.
